state.source: A slow-moving low-pressure system will bring periods of rain to the Cascadia Valley region beginning Thursday evening and continuing through Saturday afternoon. Rainfall totals are expected to range from 1.5 to 2.5 inches across the valley floor, with higher elevations along the eastern ridgeline potentially seeing up to 4 inches combined with snow above 5,000 feet. Wind gusts will pick up Friday, reaching 35 to 40 mph along exposed ridgelines, though valley winds should stay below 20 mph. Temperatures will drop from the mid-50s on Thursday to the low 40s by Saturday morning. A wind advisory is in effect for the eastern ridgeline from Friday at 6 a.m. through Saturday at noon. Motorists traveling mountain passes should expect reduced visibility and possible chain requirements above 4,500 feet starting Friday night. The system is expected to clear out by Sunday, with drier conditions and partial sun returning by midweek. River levels along the Tamsin River are being monitored, as the combination of rain and snowmelt could push flows above the minor flood stage by early next week if the heaviest rainfall bands stall over the upper watershed.
state.claim: Higher elevations along the eastern ridgeline are expected to receive more precipitation than the valley floor.

state.source: A team at the Averlin Institute for Marine Studies published findings this month on the migratory behavior of the speckled hornfish (Cyprinodon averlinensis) along the northern coastal shelf. Using satellite tags attached to 62 individuals over an eighteen-month period, researchers documented a consistent seasonal migration pattern: tagged fish moved northward into cooler waters during summer months, with peak movement occurring between late June and early August, and returned to warmer southern spawning grounds by late October. Water temperature was the strongest correlate of migration timing, with movement onset occurring within days of the shelf water crossing 18°C. Notably, the study found no significant difference in migration distance between male and female individuals, a finding that contradicts earlier, smaller-sample studies suggesting females travel farther. Tag retention was high, with 54 of the 62 units providing usable data through the full study period. The authors note that dietary data, collected via stomach content analysis on a small opportunistic subsample, suggest a shift toward crustacean prey during the northern phase of migration, though they caution this finding requires further sampling before firm conclusions can be drawn. Funding for the study was provided through a coastal research grant administered by the regional fisheries commission.
state.claim: The study found that female speckled hornfish migrate significantly farther than males.

Findings from the Solheim Glacier survey, released this week:
- Ice thickness measured at the central monitoring station: 212 meters, down from 227 meters five years ago

state.source: The forecast office is calling for what they're branding a 'significant snow event' across the Tri-Valley region this weekend, though if you've lived here longer than a winter or two you'll know to take that with a grain of salt. Current models suggest the northern valley, roughly the area above Route 12, has a decent chance of seeing 4 to 8 inches of snow starting Friday night, while the southern valley, where most of us actually live, is more likely to see a wintry mix that turns to rain by Saturday afternoon if temperatures run even a degree or two warmer than expected, which, let's be honest, happens about half the time with these forecasts. Some of the higher foothill communities could see accumulating snow linger into Sunday, but forecasters themselves admit there's meaningful uncertainty in exactly where the rain-snow line settles. The one thing that does seem fairly certain is a sharp temperature drop Friday night, with lows falling into the teens across most of the region regardless of precipitation type. Road crews have been pre-treating major routes since Thursday, and schools in the northern district have already announced a two-hour delay for Monday, snow or no snow, apparently just to be safe. As always, we'll believe the actual totals when we see them out the window.
state.claim: The entire Tri-Valley region is expected to receive accumulating snow this weekend.

state.source: What a night at Copperfield Arena! state.source: So this is a funny one because my nephew is doing his PhD at the Calloway Institute and he's been going on about this study for months at every family dinner, practically since Thanksgiving, honestly I could probably recite the abstract at this point. Anyway, the team he's part of was looking into whether a compound derived from a particular mangrove fungus, they call it CAL-19 for short, could suppress inflammation in lab mice with induced joint swelling. They ran the trial over ten weeks with three dosage groups plus a control group, and the headline result, which my nephew is very proud of because he helped run some of the imaging, was that CAL-19 did reduce measurable joint swelling at the two higher doses compared to control, by about a third on average. But — and this is the part he kept emphasizing, almost like he was worried people would get the wrong idea — the compound did not produce any detectable change in the mice's liver enzyme levels across any of the dosage groups, which the team considered an important early signal about the compound's safety profile, since liver toxicity has sunk a lot of promising anti-inflammatory compounds in earlier animal studies. He said the next phase, assuming the grant renews, will look at longer exposure windows to see if that liver safety picture holds up over time, but for now, at least in this ten-week study, the liver findings were reassuring.
state.claim: The study found that CAL-19 caused detectable changes in the mice's liver enzyme levels.

state.source: The Denholt Museum of Applied Sciences has completed installation of its new exhibit, 'Mechanisms of Flight,' spanning the museum's east wing. The exhibit comprises 34 individual displays tracing the development of powered flight from early gliders through modern commercial turbofan engines. Of the 34 displays, 21 include interactive components, such as manually operable control surface models and a wind-tunnel demonstration station, while the remaining 13 are static displays consisting of scale models, archival photographs, and period documents on loan from the regional aviation heritage society. Climate control within the exhibit hall has been upgraded to maintain the narrow humidity range required by the archival paper materials, per the loan agreement's conservation terms. The museum's exhibit design team has indicated that a subset of the interactive stations, specifically those involving the wind-tunnel demonstration, will be temporarily closed on a rotating basis for routine maintenance approximately once per month, though the museum has not yet published the specific maintenance schedule. General admission includes access to the full exhibit; no separate ticket is required. The museum anticipates the exhibit will remain installed through at least the end of next year, though this is subject to renewal of certain loan agreements with the aviation heritage society, several of which are set to expire around that time.
state.claim: Some of the interactive stations in 'Mechanisms of Flight' will be periodically closed for maintenance.

state.source: weather update for the coastal region, tuesday morning. a strong storm system sitting offshore is expected to bring heavy rain and gusty wind starting tonite and lasting thru thursday. rainfall totals along the immediate coast could reach 3 to 5 inches, inland areas east of the ridge will see less, maybe 1 to 2 inches total. wind gusts along the coast could hit 50 mph at times tonite and wednesday, strong enough to knock down tree branches and cause some power outages in exposed areas. a high surf advisory is also in effect thru thursday evening, waves could reach 12 to 15 feet at exposed beaches, officials are warning people to stay off jettys and rocky areas during this time. temps will stay mild thru the whole event, highs in the upper 50s, lows around 48. by friday the storm moves out and skies clear up, sunny and calmer conditions expected for the weekend with highs back in the low 60s. local emergency management already opened a sandbag station at the fire station on Route 9 for residents in the low lying flood zone near the harbor. school district hasnt announced any closures yet but says theyll make a call by wednesday morning depending on how bad road conditions get overnite. drivers are being told to avoid the coast highway during high tide periods wednesday and thursday due to possible wave overtopping in a couple low spots thats happened before during storms like this one.

state.source: The forecast models are, once again, in one of their moods, so take the following with the usual grain of salt. There's a system spinning up in the Pacific that could — and I stress could — bring a significant snowfall event to the higher elevations of the Cascadia range by the weekend, with some of the more excitable models cranking out numbers north of two feet above 6,000 feet. The valley floor, where most of us actually have to drive to work, is a much murkier picture; some runs show a light dusting, others show nothing at all, and honestly the forecast office's own discussion admits the valley outcome hinges on a temperature threshold that's still too close to call four days out. What does seem more consistent across the model runs is a period of gusty wind Friday into Saturday, regardless of how the precipitation shakes out, so if you've got anything not nailed down in your yard, this would be the week to deal with it. The ski resorts up at Tannerhollow are, unsurprisingly, thrilled about the possibility of a big dump, and I wouldn't be shocked if they start pre-marketing 'storm conditions' before a single flake has fallen, because that's just what they do. For the rest of us in the valley, my honest read, for whatever that's worth, is plan for wind, hope for snow, and don't be shocked if it all falls apart by Thursday night like these things so often do around here.
state.claim: Significant snowfall at higher elevations of the Cascadia range this weekend is possible but not certain.

state.source: At its regular session on the ninth of the month, the Corvingham City Council reviewed the proposed amendment to the zoning ordinance governing accessory dwelling units (ADUs) within single-family residential zones. The proposed amendment would have permitted ADUs of up to 800 square feet on lots exceeding 6,000 square feet, subject to standard setback requirements. Following a public comment period during which eleven residents spoke, split roughly evenly between support and opposition, the council voted 4-3 to table the amendment pending additional analysis from the planning department regarding projected impacts on neighborhood parking capacity and stormwater runoff. Council members Whitfield, Okafor, and Bryson voted against tabling, preferring to proceed to an immediate vote on the amendment itself; the remaining four members, including Council President Damrell, voted in favor of tabling. The planning department has been directed to return its supplemental parking analysis within 60 days, at which point the amendment will be placed back on the council's agenda for further consideration. No timeline beyond the 60-day window has been established for a final vote on the underlying amendment.
state.claim: The Corvingham City Council approved the accessory dwelling unit zoning amendment.

state.source:
Summary of findings, Kestrowick Soil Survey:
- Heavy metal contamination was not detected in soil samples taken from the northern test plots, which sit farthest from the old rail yard
- Southern plots showed elevated lead levels, consistent with prior industrial use
- Follow-up remediation planning will focus only on the southern plots
state.claim: No heavy metal contamination was found in the northern test plots.

state.source: got the mid-year report from my daughter's school today and didn't have time to read the whole thing until after the kids were in bed, but the gist is that the school added a new after-school coding club this semester and something like 60 kids signed up in the first two weeks alone, way more than the 20 the teacher running it originally expected, so now they're apparently looking for a second volunteer instructor to help split the group.
state.claim: The new after-school coding club attracted more students than the instructor initially expected.
